title: Coarse-grained vs fine-grained locking — concurrency trade-off, lock ordering makes fine-grained safe
shortTitle: Coarse-grained vs fine-grained locking — concurrency trade-off, lock ordering makes fine-grained safe

s1_definition.profdef: **Coarse-grained locking** = ONE lock protects ALL shared state. Simple to implement, impossible to deadlock (one lock), but LOW concurrency — all threads serialize through ONE bottleneck. **Fine-grained locking** = separate lock PER resource (per account, per table, per row). HIGH concurrency — operations on different resources run in parallel. Risk: DEADLOCK when acquiring multiple fine-grained locks in different orders. **Fix**: consistent global lock ordering — always acquire locks in the same deterministic order (by ID, hash). Breaks circular wait → deadlock impossible. Trade-off: coarse = simple + safe + slow. Fine = complex + fast + deadlock risk (mitigated by ordering).
s1_definition.analogy: **Coarse** = ONE key for the ENTIRE bank vault. Only one teller enters at a time. Simple! But 200 tellers wait in line to enter → bottleneck! **Fine** = each account drawer has its OWN key. 200 tellers access 200 different drawers simultaneously → fast! But: Teller-1 locks drawer-A, needs drawer-B. Teller-2 locks drawer-B, needs drawer-A → DEADLOCK! Fix: rule — "always open lower-numbered drawer first." No circular wait!
s1_definition.oneliner: Coarse = 1 lock, simple, no deadlock, low concurrency (bottleneck). Fine = N locks, complex, high concurrency, deadlock risk. Fix: global lock ordering → deadlock-free fine-grained.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** **Coarse-grained locking** = ONE lock protects ALL shared state. Simple to implement, impossible to deadlock (one lock), but LOW concurrency — all threads serialize through ONE bottleneck. **Fine-grained locking** = separate lock PER resource (per account, per table, per row). HIGH concurrency — operations on different resources run in parallel. Risk: DEADLOCK when acquiring multiple fine-grained locks in different orders. **Fix**: consistent global lock ordering — always acquire locks in the same deterministic order (by ID, hash). Breaks circular wait → deadlock impossible. Trade-off: coarse = simple + safe + slow. Fine = complex + fast + deadlock risk (mitigated by ordering).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** **Coarse** = ONE key for the ENTIRE bank vault. Only one teller enters at a time. Simple! But 200 tellers wait in line to enter → bottleneck! **Fine** = each account drawer has its OWN key. 200 tellers access 200 different drawers simultaneously → fast! But: Teller-1 locks drawer-A, needs drawer-B. Teller-2 locks drawer-B, needs drawer-A → DEADLOCK! Fix: rule — "always open lower-numbered drawer first." No circular wait!

**One line to remember:** Coarse = 1 lock, simple, no deadlock, low concurrency (bottleneck). Fine = N locks, complex, high concurrency, deadlock risk. Fix: global lock ordering → deadlock-free fine-grained.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The fund transfer service used coarse-grained locking** (one `synchronized` block for all accounts). 200 concurrent transfer requests → all serialized through one lock → throughput: 2K/sec (target: 50K/sec). Fix: per-account locks with alphabetical ordering. Transfer SAV2001→CUR3001 locks CUR3001 first (alphabetically lower), then SAV2001. Another transfer FD4001→SAV5001 locks FD4001, then SAV5001 — PARALLEL with the first! Throughput: 45K/sec. Zero deadlocks (consistent ordering).

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1 (Coarse).** 50 threads, 1 lock. Transfer SAV→CUR: lock bank → debit → credit → unlock. Transfer FD→SAV: WAIT (bank locked!) → sequential. All 50K transfers through 1 lock.

**Step 2 (Fine).** Transfer SAV→CUR: lock CUR (lower ID), lock SAV → transfer → unlock both. Transfer FD→SAV: lock FD, lock SAV → PARALLEL with first transfer (different locks!). 50K transfers across 100 accounts → massive parallelism!

**Step 3 (Ordering).** Transfer SAV→CUR: lock CUR first (alphabetically lower). Reverse transfer CUR→SAV: ALSO lock CUR first! Same order → no circular wait → no deadlock!
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ COARSE-GRAINED (1 lock) ═══

  All threads: ──lock(bank)── [transfer] ──unlock── [next thread]
  SEQUENTIAL! One at a time! Bottleneck!

  ═══ FINE-GRAINED (N locks + ordering) ═══

  Thread-1: lock(CUR) → lock(SAV) → transfer → unlock
  Thread-2: lock(FD) → lock(SAV5) → transfer → unlock ← PARALLEL!
  Thread-3: lock(ACC1) → lock(ACC2) → transfer → unlock ← PARALLEL!
  Different accounts = different locks = concurrent!

  ═══ LOCK ORDERING (prevents deadlock) ═══
  Transfer A→B: lock(A) → lock(B)   (A < B alphabetically)
  Transfer B→A: lock(A) → lock(B)   (SAME order! A < B!)
  No circular wait → no deadlock!
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Lock Granularity Spectrum ═══

  ┌─ COARSE ──────────────────────────────┐
  │  1 lock for ALL resources              │
  │  Concurrency: 1 thread at a time      │
  │  Deadlock: impossible (1 lock!)       │
  │  Complexity: minimal                   │
  │  Use: prototyping, low-traffic         │
  └────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ FINE + ORDERING ─────────────────────┐
  │  1 lock per resource (account, row)    │
  │  Concurrency: N parallel operations!  │
  │  Deadlock: prevented by lock ordering! │
  │  Ordering: sort by ID before locking  │
  │  Use: high-traffic production!        │
  └────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ LOCK-FREE ───────────────────────────┐
  │  ConcurrentHashMap, AtomicInteger      │
  │  Concurrency: maximum!                │
  │  Deadlock: impossible (no locks!)     │
  │  Complexity: highest                   │
  │  Use: counters, caches, hot paths     │
  └────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Spectrum: Coarse ←→ Fine ←→ Lock-free
  Concurrency:  low          high         maximum
  Complexity:   low          medium       high
  Deadlock risk: none        with ordering: none
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Coarse-grained locking (one lock for everything): simple, no deadlock risk, but a concurrency bottleneck — all operations serialize through one lock. Fine-grained locking (lock per resource): high concurrency — operations on different resources run in parallel. Risk: acquiring multiple locks in different orders → deadlock. Fix: consistent global lock ordering — always acquire locks in the same deterministic order (alphabetical by account ID, by hash, by index). This breaks circular wait → deadlock impossible.

The trade-off: coarse = simple + safe + slow. Fine + ordering = complex + fast + safe. Lock-free (AtomicInteger, ConcurrentHashMap) = maximum concurrency, no deadlock, highest complexity. In banking: fund transfer with coarse lock → 2K transfers/sec. Fine-grained per-account locks with alphabetical ordering → 45K transfers/sec (22x faster), zero deadlocks. Money conservation verified: total across all accounts unchanged.
